姜鹏.note: Wife of Tan Zhengwen; a public-security cadre.

陈龙.note: Veteran of the Central Social Affairs Department at Yan'an; later chief of the Nanjing and other public security bureaus.

许建国.note: Public-security leader; later chief of the Tianjin bureau and a diplomat.

李士英.note: First chief of the Shanghai Municipal Public Security Bureau; later a senior procuratorial official.

罗瑞卿.note: Luo Ruiqing (1906-1978), first Minister of Public Security of the People's Republic and later PLA chief of staff; purged in 1966.

陈毅.note: Chen Yi (1901-1972), PLA marshal, first mayor of Shanghai after liberation, and later foreign minister.

杨帆.note: Deputy chief and then chief of the Shanghai Public Security Bureau; imprisoned in 1955 in the Pan Hannian and Yang Fan affair and rehabilitated after 1980.

黄凯.note: Veteran Kuomintang Central Statistics Bureau agent, interrogated by Chen Yangshan in Nanjing in 1951.

杨匏安.note: Yang Pao'an (1896-1931), an early Marxist theorist and Communist organizer, executed by the Kuomintang in Shanghai in 1931.

罗绮园.note: Luo Qiyuan (1894-1931), a leader of the Communist peasant movement, executed with Yang Pao'an and others in 1931.

邓演达.note: Deng Yanda (1895-1931), leader of the Kuomintang left and founder of the Third Party; secretly executed on Chiang Kai-shek's order in November 1931.

张冲.note: Zhang Chong (1904-1941), a Kuomintang Central Statistics figure who ran the fabricated anti-Communist notices, but who later worked for Kuomintang-Communist cooperation and became a liaison the Communists respected.

伍豪.note: An alias of Zhou Enlai, dating from his student days in the Awakening Society; the pivot of the forged 1932 renunciation notices and their rebuttal.

周少山.note: Another of Zhou Enlai's aliases, used in the lawyer's rebuttal notice.

向忠发.note: Xiang Zhongfa (1880-1931), a worker who was nominal general secretary of the Party from 1928; arrested in Shanghai in June 1931, he defected at once and was executed by the Kuomintang days later.

卢福坦.note: Lu Futan (1893-1969), a Politburo member in the early 1930s who defected to the Kuomintang after his arrest in 1932; imprisoned by the People's Republic and died in prison.

陈琮英.note: Wife of Ren Bishi and herself a veteran Party worker; arrested in 1931 but revealed nothing.

博古.note: Bo Gu, the Party name of Qin Bangxian (1907-1946); one of the Moscow-trained 'Twenty-Eight Bolsheviks' and de facto Party leader from 1931 to 1935. He died in the same 1946 air crash as Wang Ruofei, Ye Ting, and Deng Fa.

秦邦宪.note: The original name of Bo Gu.

张闻天.note: Zhang Wentian (1900-1976), also called Luo Fu; another of the Moscow-trained leaders and general secretary of the Party from 1935; later a diplomat, purged in 1959.

李竹声.note: A member of the provisional Politburo in Shanghai who defected to the Kuomintang after his arrest in 1934.

陶行知.note: Tao Xingzhi (1891-1946), a celebrated progressive educator and public figure sympathetic to the Communists.

史量才.note: Shi Liangcai (1880-1934), owner and publisher of the Shen Bao, Shanghai's leading newspaper; his growing support for resistance and civil rights led to his assassination by Kuomintang agents in November 1934.

黄慕兰.note: Huang Mulan (1907-2017), a woman Communist underground worker in Shanghai who acted as go-between to the lawyers in the Wu Hao rebuttal.

巴和.note: The source gives the French lawyer's name only in Chinese transcription (巴和); the underlying French form is not established here.

江青.note: Jiang Qing (1914-1991), Mao Zedong's wife and a leader of the 'Gang of Four'; during the Cultural Revolution she revived the old Wu Hao forgery to attack Zhou Enlai.

王亚樵.note: Wang Yaqiao (1889-1936), the celebrated 'assassin king' of Republican Shanghai, leader of a network of gunmen; the Communist underground cultivated a working relationship with him.

张国焘.note: An early Communist leader who split with the Central Committee during the Long March and later defected to the Kuomintang (1897-1979).

谭政文.note: Veteran security officer of the Central Social Affairs Department; later director of public security in Guangdong and a deputy chief procurator.

徐强.note: A veteran of the Central Special Branch imprisoned on Kang Sheng's order in Yan'an without evidence, and rehabilitated through Li Kenong's intervention.

李白.note: Li Bai (1910-1949), the Communist underground radio operator in Shanghai executed by the Kuomintang on the eve of liberation; his story inspired the film The Unfailing Radio Waves. Not to be confused with the Tang poet of the same name.

孔祥熙.note: Kong Xiangxi (1881-1967), known in the West as H. H. Kung; financier, premier, and one of the richest men of Nationalist China.

柯庆施.note: Ke Qingshi (1902-1965), then Nanjing party secretary, later mayor of Shanghai and a Politburo member noted for his radical leftism.

穆欣.note: Mu Xin (1920-2010), journalist and author of the biography General Chen Geng.

宋庆龄.note: Song Qingling (1893-1981), widow of Sun Yat-sen and a leading non-Communist ally of the left.

陈昌.note: An underground worker who served with Chen Yangshan in Sichuan; wrongly branded a suspected agent after liberation, expelled from the Party, and driven to his death in 1960, then posthumously rehabilitated in 1961.

王世英.note: Wang Shiying (1905-1968), a veteran of Communist intelligence and united-front work who had directed underground operations in the southwest.

赵鸿飞.note: A cousin by marriage who sheltered Chen Yangshan from Kuomintang arrest in 1928.

俞胜章.note: A relative and Shanghai businessman who gave Chen Yangshan money and cover during his Special Branch years.

史良.note: Shi Liang (1900-1985), a noted woman lawyer, one of the 'Seven Gentlemen' arrested in 1936 for their resistance stand, and the first Minister of Justice of the People's Republic.

杨尚昆.note: Yang Shangkun (1907-1998), then head of the Party Central Committee's General Office; later purged in 1966 and, after rehabilitation, president of the People's Republic from 1988 to 1993.

安子文.note: An Ziwen (1909-1980), long the head of the Party's Central Organization Department.

童小鹏.note: A Communist cadre and photographer of the Yan'an and Chongqing years.

王若飞.note: Wang Ruofei (1896-1946), a senior Party leader killed in the April 1946 air crash together with Bo Gu, Ye Ting, and Deng Fa.

叶挺.note: Ye Ting (1896-1946), commander of the New Fourth Army, released from Kuomintang detention in 1946 and killed in the air crash of that April.

邓发.note: Deng Fa (1906-1946), a pioneer of Communist security and labor work, killed in the same 1946 air crash.

杨奇清.note: Yang Qiqing (1911-1978), a founding vice-minister of public security.

蔡顺礼.note: Cai Shunli (1906-1997), later a PLA lieutenant-general.

刘复之.note: Liu Fuzhi (1917-2013), later Minister of Public Security and Procurator-General.

六国饭店.note: A famous foreign-run hotel (Grand Hotel des Wagons-Lits) in the Legation Quarter of Beijing.

申报.note: The Shen Bao (Shanghai News), founded 1872, was the most influential Chinese newspaper of the Republican era.

觉悟.note: A progressive supplement of a Tianjin newspaper in which Zhou Enlai and members of the Awakening Society published in 1919-1920.

斗争.note: An organ of the Party Central Committee in the early 1930s.

中华苏维埃共和国.note: The Communist state proclaimed in the Jiangxi base area in November 1931, with Mao Zedong as chairman of its provisional central government.

国家政治保卫局.note: The security and intelligence organ of the Chinese Soviet Republic, established 1931.

龙华烈士灵园.note: On the site of the Kuomintang garrison prison at Longhua in Shanghai, where many Communists were executed in the 1930s.

中国农工民主党.en: the Chinese Peasants' and Workers' Democratic Party
中国农工民主党.note: One of the small legal 'democratic parties' of the People's Republic, descended from Deng Yanda's Third Party.

中央纪律检查委员会.en: the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection

中华全国总工会.en: the All-China Federation of Trade Unions

抢救运动.note: The 'Rescue the Fallen' drive of 1943, an extension of the Yan'an Rectification led by Kang Sheng, in which many cadres were coerced into false confessions of being spies; the later 'screening' undid much of the damage.

镇反运动.note: A nationwide campaign of 1950-1951 against former Kuomintang agents, secret-society heads, and other opponents of the new regime, carried out with mass mobilization and many executions.

三反.note: The 1951-1952 campaign against corruption, waste, and bureaucratism among officials.

抗美援朝.en: the War to Resist America and Aid Korea
抗美援朝.note: China's name for its intervention in the Korean War, 1950-1953.

板门店.note: The village on the Korean truce line where the armistice negotiations were held from 1951; Li Kenong headed the Chinese delegation's work there.

八大.note: The Eighth National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party, held in September 1956, which declared the main task now to be economic construction.

申江伏魔记.en: Subduing the Demons on the Shen River

ch05.anchor: come at once to Beiping for the First National Public Security Work Conference
ch05.note: The First National Public Security Work Conference, held in Beijing in the autumn of 1949, set the framework for the new state's security organs. (Beiping was the name of the city until it was renamed Beijing in October 1949; the source uses both.)

ch05.anchor: put up at the Six Nations Hotel on Zhengyi Road
ch05.note: The Six Nations Hotel (the Grand Hotel des Wagons-Lits) stood in the old Legation Quarter of Beijing and had long been a place where foreigners and Chinese officials met.

ch05.anchor: Our 'lucky general' is here
ch05.note: “Lucky general” (fujiang) is an affectionate term for a commander under whom things always seem to go well; Li Kenong uses it warmly of Chen Yangshan.

ch05.anchor: Luo Ruiqing to chief of the Beiping bureau
ch05.note: Luo Ruiqing (1906-1978) became the first Minister of Public Security of the People's Republic and later PLA chief of staff; he was purged in 1966 and rehabilitated after his death.

ch05.anchor: his wife, Zhang Suzhen, back to their home district
ch05.note: Zhang Suzhen was Chen Yangshan's wife.

ch05.anchor: the "sacred ground of six dynasties"
ch05.note: Nanjing served as capital of a succession of dynasties from the third to the sixth century (the “Six Dynasties”), and again under the Ming and the Republic; hence its reputation as an imperial city.

ch05.anchor: a veteran secret agent and traitor of the Kuomintang's Central Statistics Bureau
ch05.note: The Central Statistics Bureau (Zhongtong) was the Kuomintang party's civilian intelligence and secret-police organ, distinct from the military Juntong; it is a recurring adversary in this book.

ch05.anchor: Our Party's Central Committee member Yang Pao'an
ch05.note: Yang Pao'an (1896-1931) was one of the earliest Chinese Marxist writers; he was arrested and executed in Shanghai in 1931. His fellow martyr Luo Qiyuan (1894-1931), a leader of the peasant movement, died at the same time.

ch05.anchor: the patriot Deng Yanda
ch05.note: Deng Yanda (1895-1931), a leader of the Kuomintang left and founder of the “Third Party,” was secretly executed on Chiang Kai-shek's order in November 1931.

ch05.anchor: impersonated Wu Hao, Zhou Enlai's alias, to run a "Wu Hao Notice"
ch05.note: “Wu Hao” was a pen name Zhou Enlai had used since his student days. In 1932 the Kuomintang forged a notice in which “Wu Hao and 243 others” announced their withdrawal from the Communist Party, to discredit Zhou; the fabrication and its rebuttal are the subject of the pages that follow. The story is well documented and forms a set piece of Party history.

ch05.anchor: together with another Central Statistics agent, Zhang Chong
ch05.note: Zhang Chong (1904-1941) was a Kuomintang Central Statistics figure who took part in the anti-Communist forgeries but later, as a liaison for Kuomintang-Communist cooperation, earned the respect of Zhou Enlai and others.

ch05.anchor: only four members of the Party's Central Political Bureau remained in Shanghai
ch05.note: Xiang Zhongfa (1880-1931), a former worker, was the nominal general secretary of the Party from 1928. Arrested in Shanghai in June 1931, he defected on the spot but was executed by the Kuomintang within days.

ch05.anchor: Zhou Enlai moved swiftly to the Metropole Hotel on Simalu
ch05.note: Simalu (“Fourth Avenue”) is the old name of Fuzhou Road in Shanghai; the Metropole was a foreign-run hotel, chosen because the concession authorities limited Kuomintang police action there.

ch05.anchor: Xiang Zhongfa gave up Ren Bishi's wife, Chen Congying
ch05.note: Ren Bishi (1904-1950) was a top Party leader; his wife Chen Congying, herself a veteran underground worker, was arrested in this sweep but gave nothing away under torture.

ch05.anchor: On the proposal of the Comintern's Far Eastern Bureau
ch05.note: The Communist International (Comintern) directed the Chinese Party through its Far Eastern Bureau; the provisional Politburo it approved was dominated by the Moscow-trained group around Bo Gu.

ch05.anchor: made up of six men — Bo Gu, Zhang Wentian
ch05.note: Bo Gu (Qin Bangxian, 1907-1946) and Zhang Wentian (1900-1976) were leading figures of the Moscow-trained “Twenty-Eight Bolsheviks”; Bo Gu was de facto Party leader until the 1935 Zunyi Conference. Lu Futan and Li Zhusheng, also named here, both later defected to the Kuomintang after arrest.

ch05.anchor: He had used it for a long time
ch05.note: The Awakening (Juewu) was a progressive newspaper supplement associated with Zhou Enlai's Awakening Society in Tianjin around 1919-1920.

ch05.anchor: issue a statement in the Party Central organ Struggle
ch05.note: Struggle (Douzheng) was an organ of the Party Central Committee in the early 1930s.

ch05.anchor: chairman of the provisional central government of the Chinese Soviet Republic
ch05.note: The Chinese Soviet Republic, proclaimed in the Jiangxi base area in November 1931 with Mao Zedong as chairman, gave the Communists a rival government to the Nationalist state.

ch05.anchor: Mr. Tao Xingzhi, a democratic figure serving as adviser to the Shen Bao
ch05.note: Tao Xingzhi (1891-1946) was a celebrated progressive educator; the Shen Bao (Shanghai News) was the most influential newspaper of the Republican era.

ch05.anchor: he would go to its chairman, Shi Liangcai
ch05.note: Shi Liangcai (1880-1934), owner of the Shen Bao, backed resistance to Japan and civil rights; Kuomintang agents assassinated him in 1934. The account of his reluctance here fits his known independence, though the private exchanges the author reports cannot be independently verified.

ch05.anchor: the licensed French lawyer Ba He
ch05.note: The source names the French lawyer only in Chinese transcription (Ba He); histories of the episode identify the rebuttal notice as issued through a French lawyer in the Shanghai concessions, whose extraterritorial standing put him beyond Kuomintang reprisal. The underlying French name is not established here.

ch05.anchor: winning over Wang Yaqiao, the foremost assassin of the Republic
ch05.note: Wang Yaqiao (1889-1936) led a famous band of assassins in Republican Shanghai and mounted attempts on Chiang Kai-shek and others; the Communist underground cultivated ties with him. He was himself assassinated by Kuomintang agents in 1936.

ch05.anchor: the Panmunjom talks during the War to Resist America and Aid Korea
ch05.note: Li Kenong headed the Chinese side's work at the Korean armistice negotiations at Panmunjom (1951-1953); “the War to Resist America and Aid Korea” is China's name for its part in the Korean War.

ch05.anchor: When the American Central Intelligence Agency learned of his death
ch05.note: This often-repeated claim, that the CIA declared a holiday when Li Kenong died in 1962, circulates widely in Chinese accounts of him but rests on no verifiable source and is best read as legend rather than fact.

ch05.anchor: he put on the gleaming rank of a colonel general
ch05.note: In the People's Liberation Army's first system of ranks (1955), shangjiang corresponds to colonel general (three-star). The three orders named — of August the First, of Independence and Freedom, of Liberation — honored, respectively, service in the founding of the Red Army, the war against Japan, and the war of liberation.

ch05.anchor: he served as executive head of the State Political Security Bureau
ch05.note: The State Political Security Bureau was the security and intelligence organ of the Chinese Soviet Republic, set up in 1931.

ch05.anchor: settling the screening left over from the
ch05.note: The “Rescue” campaign of 1943, an offshoot of the Yan'an Rectification run by Kang Sheng, extracted many false confessions of espionage; the “screening” (zhenbie) that followed was the work of clearing the wrongly accused.

ch05.anchor: a villa on Yueyang Road that had once been Kong Xiangxi's
ch05.note: Kong Xiangxi (1881-1967), known in the West as H. H. Kung, was a financier and premier of Nationalist China and one of its richest men; his former Shanghai residences passed to the state after 1949.

ch05.anchor: Li Kenong's "conscientious and responsible resolving" of the political question of Xu Qiang
ch05.note: Xu Qiang, a veteran of the Central Special Branch, had been imprisoned in Yan'an on Kang Sheng's order without evidence; Li Kenong personally revised the finding to clear him.

ch05.anchor: swept the graves of Peng Pai, Lü Ming, Li Bai
ch05.note: Li Bai (1910-1949) was the Communist underground radio operator executed in Shanghai on the eve of liberation, later famous through the film The Unfailing Radio Waves; he is not the Tang poet of the same name. Peng Pai (1896-1929) was the pioneer of the Communist peasant movement, executed in Shanghai.

ch05.anchor: The Campaign to Suppress Counter-Revolutionaries launched across the country in 1951
ch05.note: This nationwide campaign of 1950-1951 struck at former Kuomintang agents, secret-society heads, and other opponents of the new order, with mass rallies and many executions; the debate over a “steady” versus a “bold and open” line was a real policy question of the day.

ch05.anchor: The party secretary, Ke Qingshi
ch05.note: Ke Qingshi (1902-1965), then Nanjing party secretary, later became mayor of Shanghai and a Politburo member known for his radical leftism.

ch05.anchor: During the "Three-Antis" campaign of 1951
ch05.note: The “Three-Antis” campaign (1951-1952) targeted corruption, waste, and bureaucratism among officials; the quota-setting the passage criticizes was a common abuse of such mass campaigns.

ch05.anchor: a magazine called Celebrity Biography, published by a press in Zhengzhou
ch05.note: The episode concerns a piece of popular reportage the author regarded as plagiarized from Mu Xin's biography General Chen Geng and padded with invention; Mu Xin (1920-2010) was a journalist and Party historian. The author's own book is thus in part a corrective to such embroidered accounts of the intelligence war.

ch05.anchor: at a meeting of the leading members of the Supreme People's Procuratorate
ch05.note: The Supreme People's Procuratorate is the state's highest organ of legal supervision and prosecution; Chen Yangshan served in the procuratorial system in his later years.

ch05.anchor: In 1935, Chen Yangshan had done underground work in Chongqing and Chengdu with Chen Chang
ch05.note: Chen Chang, wrongly branded a suspected agent after liberation and hounded to his death in 1960, was posthumously cleared in 1961 largely through Chen Yangshan's efforts — even as Chen Yangshan himself was under attack, a foretaste of the persecution recounted in the next chapter.

ch05.anchor: the leader who had sent them to Sichuan in those years
ch05.note: Wang Shiying (1905-1968), a veteran of Communist intelligence and united-front work, had directed underground operations in the southwest.

ch05.anchor: the "anti-Party clique" case of the Ministry of Justice's Party group had been reviewed by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection
ch05.note: In 1958 Chen Yangshan was caught up, with others of the Ministry of Justice's Party group, in a fabricated “anti-Party clique” case and stripped of his posts; the wrong was formally reviewed only years later. Chapter Six tells this story in full.

ch05.anchor: place him as a vice-chairman in Inner Mongolia or Ningxia
ch05.note: Vice-chairman is the deputy head of the government of an autonomous region (the counterpart of a provincial vice-governor); Chen Yangshan was finally posted to Ningxia in 1966, on the eve of the Cultural Revolution.

ch05.anchor: joined the Chinese Peasants' and Workers' Democratic Party
ch05.note: One of the small legal “democratic parties” of the People's Republic, descended from Deng Yanda's Third Party; membership marked a non-Communist figure aligned with the regime.

ch05.anchor: the noted jurist Minister Shi Liang
ch05.note: Shi Liang (1900-1985) was a celebrated woman lawyer, one of the “Seven Gentlemen” arrested in 1936 for their anti-Japanese stand, and the first Minister of Justice of the People's Republic.

ch05.anchor: Comrade Shangkun and Comrade Xiaoping
ch05.note: Yang Shangkun (1907-1998), then head of the Party Central Committee's General Office, and Deng Xiaoping. An Ziwen (1909-1980), named below, headed the Central Organization Department.

ch05.anchor: Bolshevik greetings
ch05.note: “Bolshevik greetings” (bu li) was a standard closing in Party correspondence of the period.

ch05.anchor: arranged for them to enjoy the middle-mess ration
ch05.note: Cadres and their dependents in the base areas were fed by grade — the “large,” “middle,” and “small” messes; Chen Yangshan refused the better ration for his children.

ch05.anchor: limited to the chief responsible comrades of the public security departments
ch05.note: The source here prints 西安 (Xi'an) where the sense plainly requires 公安 (public security); an evident misprint, corrected in this rendering.

ch05.anchor: his cousin came to Beijing to visit
ch05.note: The source refers to this relative as a paternal older cousin (tangxiong) twice and, in the next paragraph, once as a wife's older brother (qixiong); rendered consistently here as his cousin, the more frequent reading, which also agrees with the later mention of the man's wife as Chen Yangshan's cousin's wife.
